evidence.title: Towards Safe AI Clinicians: A Comprehensive Study on Large Language Model Jailbreaking in Healthcare
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.outcome: Vulnerability of seven LLMs to black-box jailbreaking attacks in medical contexts
evidence.effect: Leading commercial and open-source LLMs were highly vulnerable to three medical jailbreaking techniques; no numeric results reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Experiment results indicate that leading commercial and open-source LLMs are highly vulnerable to medical jailbreaking attacks.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether continuous security monitoring or scheduled red-teaming of generative AI reduces cyberattacks, data exfiltration, jailbreaks, or misuse in health care. One benchmark study reports that seven commercial and open-source language models were highly vulnerable to medical jailbreaking techniques, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that red-teaming prevents it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and one hazard study. That study is an automated benchmark of seven language models, rated level 5, and its abstract reports no numeric results. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice cannot be rated because no comparison of monitored and unmonitored deployments exists. The four endorsements are frameworks and a commentary.

Seven language models were highly vulnerable to three medical jailbreaking techniques in a benchmark setting. This suggests that guardrails may fail under deliberate manipulation, which could produce unsafe clinical content. Red-teaming is designed to find such failures before patients see them, but no study shows how many real-world failures it catches or how often vulnerabilities reappear after model updates.

NIST AI 600-1 states that documenting and reviewing third-party inputs and plugins is important for incident disclosure, because plugin content often has inconsistent access control. CHAI guidance describes network baselines and expected data flows. These documents set expectations that health systems may be asked to meet, but they rest on expert consensus rather than outcome data.

The CHAI playbook describes one academic medical center that runs a dedicated AI security function with continuous API monitoring, quarterly adversarial assessments for high-risk AI, and sector threat-intelligence sharing. The sources report no staffing levels, costs, or yield of findings. Smaller systems would have to estimate the burden of this model without published figures.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployed clinical AI with and without scheduled red-teaming and continuous monitoring, and that report the number of vulnerabilities found, incidents prevented, time to remediation after model updates, and staff hours and cost per assessment.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the single hazard study was a model benchmark that did not involve any patient population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether jailbreaks succeed more often through non-English or low-literacy prompts, and whether safety-net systems can afford ongoing red-teaming, remains untested.
